methodology_note: This was NOT sourced by scraping news, Reddit, or forums -- deliberately. That approach would have (1) a severe selection bias, since routine/everyday discrimination is specifically the kind of thing that does NOT make news (only severe or unusual incidents do, which would represent the extreme tail, not the 'how common' baseline); (2) no denominator, since a scraped incident count cannot produce a prevalence rate the way asking a representative sample of households can; (3) a demographic skew toward urban, English-speaking, internet-connected populations, unrepresentative of where this practice has been found most prevalent (rural India); and (4) real consent/privacy concerns around aggregating people's personal accounts of caste identity and discrimination without their knowledge. A nationally representative household survey is the correct instrument for a prevalence question, and IHDS-II already did this at scale (~42,000 households).

source.paper: Thorat, Amit and Joshi, Omkar (2020). 'The Continuing Practice of Untouchability in India: Patterns and Mitigating Influences.' Economic & Political Weekly, Vol LV, No 2, January 11, 2020.
source.underlying_survey: India Human Development Survey, Round II (IHDS-II), 2011-12. NCAER (National Council of Applied Economic Research) and University of Maryland. ~42,000 households, nationally representative.
source.single_round_caveat: This is a single-round snapshot (2011-12), not a trend -- IHDS-III field data collection completed June 2024, but as of this writing no published analysis of the untouchability-practice question from that round could be found. A future update could add a second data point if/when IHDS-III results on this question are published.

table1_practice_by_social_group.question: Does any member of your household practise untouchability?
table1_practice_by_social_group.note: This is Table 1 in the source paper. Its own stated 'Total' (21%) differs from the paper's separately-stated prose headline figure of 27% overall -- both come from the same paper; the discrepancy is in the source itself, not introduced here. Both are reported.

table2_specific_practice.question: Is it a problem if an SC enters the kitchen or uses utensils?
table2_specific_practice.note: A more specific, behavioral question (vs. Table 1's general framing) -- asked of non-SC respondents about a concrete scenario. This is Table 2 in the source paper.

income_quintile.note: 10 percentage point gap, poorest to richest quintile -- a much smaller gradient than the caste-group gradient, suggesting the practice is not simply a function of income.

regional.note: Broad multi-state regions, not individual states -- exact state-wise figures were not given as a numeric table in the source paper, only this regional breakdown.
regional.south_east_west_note: Described in the source only as having the 'lowest incidences' -- no single combined percentage was stated for this grouping.
